title: Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) treatment in adolescent depression
official: Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) treatment in adolescent depression
summary:
Background and study aims
Depression can have a major effect on young people’s mood, daily life and wellbeing. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) is a non-invasive treatment that uses a weak electrical current delivered through a headset to stimulate particular areas of the brain. Studies in adults suggest that tDCS may help reduce symptoms of depression, but less is known about its use at home in adolescents. This study will investigate whether a 10-week course of home-based tDCS is acceptable, feasible and safe for adolescents with depression. It will also explore whether tDCS may be associated with changes in depressive symptoms and brain activity.

Who can participate?
Young people aged 15 to 19 years with a diagnosis of major depressive disorder and mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms, who are under the care of a GP and/or Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services. Participants aged 15 will also need consent from a parent or guardian.

What does the study involve?
Participants will first complete a screening assessment to check whether the study is suitable for them. Those who are eligible will continue their usual treatment and will be randomly allocated, with an equal chance, to receive either active tDCS or sham tDCS. Sham tDCS is designed to feel similar at the start of a session but does not provide ongoing stimulation. Participants will use tDCS device at home after training from the research team. The first session will be supported in person or by video call. Participants will complete 36 sessions over 10 weeks, with each session lasting 30 minutes. During this period, neither participants nor the researchers carrying out the assessments will know which treatment has been allocated. Participants will complete assessments about their mood, wellbeing, treatment experience and possible side effects before, during and after the 10-week treatment period. Some participants may also complete an EEG assessment to measure brain activity. After 10 weeks, participants will be told which treatment they received and will be offered a further 10-week period of active tDCS. A final follow-up assessment will take place eight months after randomisation.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may or may not experience an improvement in their symptoms. Taking part may help researchers understand whether home-based tDCS could become a useful treatment option for young people with depression. Possible side effects of tDCS are usually mild and temporary. They can include redness, tingling, itching or discomfort under the electrodes, and headache. There is also a small risk of an unusually elevated mood. Participants will be monitored by the research team and will be able to contact them if they have any concerns.

Where is the study run from?
The study is run by the Department of Psychology at the University of East London. Participants will complete the tDCS sessions at home, with remote support from the research team.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to December 2028.

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by Rosetrees Trust and the University of East London through a PhD scholarship.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	Adolescents aged 15 to 19 years
2.	Having a diagnosis of major depressive disorder as made by a GP or psychiatrist (e.g., GP services, CAMHS)
3.	Having mild to moderate severity of depressive symptoms as measured by a score of 12 to 34 on the MADRS rating scale
4.	Being medication-free, or taking medication or in psychotherapy, for at least 6 weeks before enrolment
5.	Being under the care of a GP and/or CAMHS
6.	Agreeable for GP to be regularly informed by the research team about participation
7.	Agreeable to have a structured clinical assessment, such as Mini-International Neuropsychiatric Interview Kid (MINI-Kid) for 15-17 years old or MINI for 18-19 years old, for Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria
8.	Able to provide written, informed consent if 16 years old and above, or able to provide Assent if 15 years old and with parental or guardian written, informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Significant suicide risk as measured by answering 'yes' to questions 4, 5 or 6b on the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) Screen (Posner et al., 2011)
2.	Primary comorbid psychiatric disorder (e.g., obsessive-compulsive disorder) based on DSM-5 criteria as assessed in MINI-Kid or MINI (Sheehan et al., 1998)
3.	Having a severe depression as measured by a score of above 34 on the MADRS
4.	Current daily use of medications that affect cortical excitability (e.g., benzodiazepines)
5.	History of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), other brain stimulation, or psychosurgery for depression
6.	History of esketamine / ketamine for treatment of depression
7.	Medical disorder that may mimic mood disorder (e.g., hormonal disorder)
8.	Have cognitive impairment
9.	History of a neurological disorder (e.g., structural lesion, epilepsy, seizures)
10.	History of migraines or intractable headaches
11.	Implant in the brain, neurocranial defect, active implantable medical device or any ferromagnetic material in the head
